free.question: Is QRdx really free? Are there hidden limits?
free.answer: Yes. Creating, customizing and downloading static QR codes is free and needs no account: unlimited codes, every design option ({bodyPatterns, number} body patterns, {eyeShapes, number} corner-eye shapes and {eyeCentres, number} eye centers, gradients, logos, frames and Logo QR or Image QR art), and PNG, JPG, SVG, PDF and EPS downloads. There are no watermarks and no ads. Static codes store your content in the code itself, so they never expire and have no scan limits. A free account adds 10 dynamic QR codes, 3 hosted pages, 90 days of scan analytics, 10 saved themes and 5 AI theme generations; Pro ({proMonthly}/mo or {proYearly}/yr) and Business ({businessMonthly}/mo or {businessYearly}/yr) raise those limits.

signup.question: Do I need to sign up or create an account?
signup.answer: Not for static codes. Open the playground, enter your URL or content, customize the design and download it without signing up. Sign in (with GitHub or Google) when you want dynamic codes you can edit after printing, hosted pages, scan analytics, saved themes, community publishing or AI theme generation.

dynamic.question: Does QRdx support dynamic QR codes and scan analytics?
dynamic.answer: Yes. A dynamic code encodes a short link, so you can change where it points after printing, and every scan is counted with country, device and browser analytics. A code can open a website or a hosted mobile page (link list, menu, vCard, coupon, event, form, PDF, gallery, audio or video). Pro and Business add smart routing by device, country, language or time, A/B tests, UTM tags, passwords, expiry dates and scan limits. Free accounts get 10 active dynamic codes with 90 days of history; Pro and Business are unlimited with longer history.

guarantee.question: Will my QR codes stop working if I stop paying?
guarantee.answer: No. Under our Never-Hostage Guarantee every dynamic code keeps redirecting on every plan, including after a downgrade, a failed payment or a cancellation. Scans are unlimited and never paused, and we never show ads or send your scanners to a QRdx page. Plan limits only stop you creating new things. Static codes don't depend on QRdx at all.

compare.question: How does QRdx compare to QR Tiger, QR Code Monkey, or Flowcode?
compare.answer: QR TIGER and Flowcode are dynamic QR platforms: codes redirect through their service so you can edit them and track scans, and pricing grows with the number of codes. QR TIGER's free plan includes 3 dynamic codes with 500 scans each, and Flowcode's free plan allows 2 codes. QR Code Monkey, like QRdx, makes free static codes. QRdx does both: unlimited free static codes with deep styling, plus dynamic codes with unlimited scans on every plan, paid plans from {proMonthly} a month, and open-source code you can self-host. Our compare pages cover each tool in detail, including where it is the better choice.

logo.question: Can I add a logo to my QR code for free?
logo.answer: Yes. Logo overlay is included on the free tier. Upload an image (a PNG with a transparent background works best) and QRdx centers it and clears the modules underneath. QR codes use Reed-Solomon error correction (ISO/IEC 18004); QRdx defaults to level Q, which can recover roughly 25% of the code, so a centered logo stays scannable. Test with a few phones before printing.

openSource.question: Is QRdx open source?
openSource.answer: Yes. QRdx is open source under the GNU AGPL-3.0 (or later) and developed in public on GitHub. You can review the code, file issues, contribute, or self-host your own instance, dynamic codes and hosted pages included. The QR library is published on npm as qrdx for React apps. AGPL is a copyleft license, so check that it fits your project before embedding it in closed-source software.

api.question: Can developers generate QR codes with an API?
api.answer: Yes. The image API turns any URL into an SVG, PNG or EPS QR code with no API key, and the REST API, with a workspace API key or OAuth, creates and edits dynamic codes and reads their scans. There is also an MCP server for Claude, Cursor and VS Code, a command-line tool (@qrdx/cli), a shadcn/ui component and the qrdx React library.

cancel.question: What happens if I cancel?
cancel.answer: Nothing breaks. Your plan stays active until the end of the period you paid for, then your account moves to Free. Every dynamic code keeps redirecting and every scan is still counted: that's our Never-Hostage Guarantee. On Free you can't create more than the Free limits allow, and analytics show the last 90 days.

paymentFails.question: What happens if a payment fails?
paymentFails.answer: Your codes keep working. If the subscription lapses, your account follows the Free limits, exactly as if you had cancelled. We never pause codes, show ads, or send your scanners to a QRdx page because of billing.

scans.question: Do scans count against a limit?
scans.answer: No. Scans are unlimited on every plan and we never pause a code because of traffic. The only scan caps are the ones you set yourself on a code (Pro and Business).

rupees.question: Why do I see prices in ₹?
rupees.answer: Visitors from India see prices in Indian rupees: Pro is {proMonthly} a month or {proYearly} a year, Business {businessMonthly} a month or {businessYearly} a year. Checkout charges customers in India in ₹ and everyone else in US$, whichever currency you browsed in. Use the switch above the plans to change the display currency.

switchPlans.question: Can I switch plans or billing periods later?
switchPlans.answer: Yes. Open Manage subscription in your settings to change or cancel your plan in the Polar billing portal. Moving to a smaller plan never turns off existing codes, pages or domains.

teams.question: How do teams work on each plan?
teams.answer: Free accounts can't create teams. A Pro team has up to 3 members including the owner; a Business team has no member limit. A team's limits follow the best plan among its owners, and existing members stay if that plan changes.

selfHost.question: Can I self-host instead?
selfHost.answer: Yes. QRdx is open source under the AGPL-3.0. Run it with your own Postgres database by following the self-hosting guide; the plan limits are defined in one file that you can change for your instance.

faq.benefitQuestion: Which industries benefit most from QR codes?
faq.benefitAnswer: Any business that prints something a customer holds or walks past: menus, packaging, signs, tickets, labels and direct mail. The return is highest where information changes after printing (menus, prices, schedules, documents), because a dynamic code updates without a reprint.
faq.staticQuestion: Should a business use static or dynamic QR codes?
faq.staticAnswer: Use static codes for content that never changes, such as a Wi-Fi login, a payment ID or a contact card, because they are free and work without any service in between. Use dynamic codes for anything printed in volume or kept for months, so you can fix a wrong link, change the destination and measure scans.
faq.cancelQuestion: Do QRdx codes stop working if I cancel?

faq.sizeQuestion: How big should a QR code be?
faq.sizeAnswer: About a tenth of the distance it is scanned from, a little more for denser codes: roughly 2.5 to 3 cm for a card held in the hand, 23 cm for a poster 2 m away and about 70 cm for a sign 6 m away. Keep each module at least 0.4 mm and leave a blank margin of four modules around the code.
faq.failQuestion: What makes a printed QR code fail to scan?
faq.failAnswer: The usual causes are low contrast (pale or inverted colours), a missing quiet zone, printing too small for the distance, glare from glossy finishes, and placement on curves, folds or seams. Test the printed proof, not just the file.
faq.formatQuestion: Which file format should I send to the printer?
faq.formatAnswer: Vector: SVG or a print-ready CMYK PDF, both free from QRdx. Vectors stay sharp at any size, from a 2 cm label to a 2 m banner.

A 512 px PNG takes about 20 ms on a laptop, so the full {rows, number} take a few minutes. Bigger PNGs take longer and make bigger files, so choose 512 px unless you need more.
faq.rowAnswer: Any text up to the QR code limit: links, plain text, or payloads such as WIFI:..., mailto:..., tel:... and BEGIN:VCARD. The content is encoded exactly as it appears in the cell.
faq.staticQuestion: Are the generated codes static or dynamic?

printSize.metaDescription: Find the minimum printed size for a QR code from the scanning distance, the data it holds and its error-correction level. Results in mm and inches.
printSize.title: QR code print size calculator
printSize.intro1: Printed too small, a QR code fails exactly where it matters: on a poster across the room, a sign by the road or a label on a crowded shelf. Enter how far away people will scan from and what the code contains, and the calculator works out the smallest size that will still scan reliably.
printSize.intro2: It goes beyond the simple distance ÷ 10 rule by accounting for how dense your code is: a long link or a vCard needs more modules than a short URL, so each module, and the whole code, must be printed bigger.
printSize.how1: The content decides the QR version. The calculator picks the smallest version (1 to 40) that holds your text at the chosen error-correction level, using the same capacity tables as the QRdx encoder. Version n is 17 + 4n modules wide.
printSize.how2: The distance decides the module size. The {ratio, number}:1 rule of thumb is treated as describing a simple {reference, number, ::group-off} × {reference, number} code, so each module must be at least distance ÷ ({divisor, number}), and never less than {minimum, number} mm.
printSize.how3: Module size × modules per side gives the code size. Adding {quiet, number} blank modules on each side gives the space the code needs on the page.
printSize.tip1: Keep the content short. A shorter link means a lower version, so the same printed size gives bigger modules.
printSize.tip2: Use dark modules on a light background with strong contrast; inverted or pastel codes fail on some scanners.
printSize.tip3: Test the printed code with several phones at the real distance and lighting before a large print run.
printSize.tip4: Need a code first? Use the <generators>QR code generators</generators> or the <editor>full editor</editor>, then export as SVG for print.

faq.minimumQuestion: What is the minimum size for a QR code?
faq.minimumAnswer: It depends on how far away people scan from and how dense the code is. For a short link scanned from about 25 cm, around 2.5 cm (1 inch) is enough. Whatever the distance, keep each module at least {minimum, number} mm wide so printers and cameras can resolve it.
faq.ruleQuestion: What is the 10:1 rule for QR codes?
faq.ruleAnswer: A common rule of thumb is that a QR code can be scanned from about ten times its width, so a 10 cm code works from about 1 m. It assumes a fairly simple code; codes with more data need to be printed larger, which is what this calculator adjusts for.
faq.logoQuestion: Does a logo or higher error correction change the size?
faq.logoAnswer: Higher error correction adds redundancy, so the same content needs a higher version with more modules, and therefore a larger print. A logo doesn't change the module count, but it hides modules, so use level Q or H when adding one.
faq.quietQuestion: Does the quiet zone count towards the size?
faq.quietAnswer: The code size shown is edge to edge. Scanners also need a blank margin of {quiet, number} modules on every side, which the second figure includes. QRdx downloads have no margin unless you turn on the quiet zone, so leave that space around the code in your layout.
faq.resolutionQuestion: What resolution should I export for print?
faq.resolutionAnswer: Use SVG when you can: it is vector and stays sharp at any size. For PNG, export at least the pixel width shown for 300 DPI, which is the usual minimum for print.

scanChecker.metaDescription: Add a picture of a QR code to read it and test how reliably it scans at small sizes, with blur and low contrast. Runs in your browser; nothing is uploaded.
scanChecker.title: QR code scan checker
scanChecker.intro1: Will it scan? Upload, drop or paste a screenshot or photo of any QR code to see what it contains and how reliably it reads, before it goes on a menu, poster or package.
scanChecker.intro2: The checker decodes the code, then shrinks and blurs it the way a phone camera would and tests it again at several sizes, with checks for contrast, clear space and resolution. Everything happens in your browser.
scanChecker.test1: Decoding at 96, 160 and 320 pixels wide with simulated camera blur: roughly a small or distant print, normal phone distance and a close-up.
scanChecker.test2: Contrast between the dark and light modules, measured from the image pixels.
scanChecker.test3: Polarity: light codes on dark backgrounds are not read by every scanner app.
scanChecker.test4: Clear space (the quiet zone) around the code, when the image shows it.
scanChecker.test5: Image resolution: how many pixels each module gets.
scanChecker.design: The <editor>QRdx editor</editor> shows a live scan score while you design, flags risky eye shapes and oversized logos, and exports print-ready vector PDFs. Use the <size>print size calculator</size> to choose how big to print it.

faq.uploadAnswer: No. The checker runs entirely in your browser with JavaScript. The image is read on your device and never sent to a server.
faq.scoreQuestion: How is the scan score calculated?
faq.scoreAnswer: The checker finds the code with the open-source jsQR decoder, shrinks it to 96, 160 and 320 pixels wide, adds camera-like blur and contrast loss, and tries to decode it a few times at each size. It then measures the contrast between dark and light modules, whether the code is dark on light, the clear space around it and the image resolution. Each problem lowers the score from 100.
faq.lowQuestion: My code scores low but scans on my phone. Why?
faq.lowAnswer: Phone camera apps are often more forgiving than jsQR, and a photo can lose contrast or sharpness that the printed code doesn't. Treat a low score as a warning that weaker scanners, smaller prints or poor lighting may fail, and test-scan with a few phones before a big print run.
faq.sizeQuestion: How big should a printed QR code be?
faq.sizeAnswer: A common rule of thumb is width ≈ scanning distance ÷ 10, so a code scanned from 20 cm should be about 2 cm wide. Codes holding more data need to be bigger; the print size calculator works it out for you.
faq.fixQuestion: How do I fix a low score?
faq.fixAnswer: Use a dark code on a light background with strong contrast, keep clear space around the code, pick simple square or rounded eyes, choose a higher error-correction level if there is a logo, shorten the content, or print it bigger.

faq.howQuestion: How do I scan a QR code online?
faq.howAnswer: Open this page, tap Start camera and allow camera access, then point your camera at the code. On a laptop or when the code is already on your screen, switch to Image and upload, drag in or paste a screenshot. The result appears under the scanner. Links never open until you tap Open.
faq.safeQuestion: Is it safe to open a link from a QR code?
faq.safeAnswer: Usually, but fake QR codes stuck over real ones ("quishing") are a common scam. Before you open a link, the scanner follows its redirects (up to five) to show where it really ends up{webRisk, select, yes {, checks each address with Google Web Risk} other {}} and looks for common tricks: lookalike letters from other alphabets, bare IP addresses, link shorteners, a fake site name hidden before an @, brand names on unrelated domains, unencrypted pages and app downloads. No check catches everything, so still be careful with sign-in and payment pages.
faq.verifiedAnswer: The link is a real, active dynamic QR code created with QRdx (a qrdx.dev/q/ link{domains, select, yes { or a verified custom domain} other {}}) and has no open abuse reports. It tells you the code is genuine and hasn't been switched off; the code's owner still decides where it points, so the other safety checks still apply.
faq.privateQuestion: Are my scans uploaded or saved?
faq.privateAnswer: No. Camera frames and images are decoded in your browser and never leave your device. Your scan history is stored only in this browser (IndexedDB); you can turn it off, delete single scans or clear it all. To preview a link, only that address is sent to QRdx{webRisk, select, yes { and Google Web Risk} other {}}, and QRdx doesn't keep it. What you scan is kept out of site analytics.
faq.wifiQuestion: Why can't the scanner join a Wi-Fi network for me?
faq.wifiAnswer: Web browsers aren't allowed to change your device's Wi-Fi settings. The scanner shows the network name and lets you copy the password, so you can paste it in your Wi-Fi settings. Your phone's built-in camera app can usually join a Wi-Fi QR code directly.
faq.batchQuestion: Can I scan many codes in a row?
faq.batchAnswer: Yes. Turn on Batch mode and keep pointing the camera at codes, or add several images at once. Each new code is added to the list once, and you can export the batch, or your whole history, as a CSV file.
faq.offlineAnswer: Once you've scanned with it, your browser keeps the scanner page and its decoder, so it opens and reads codes without a connection. Link safety checks need a connection, and links found offline can be checked later from your history.
faq.browsersAnswer: Any modern browser with camera access: Chrome, Edge, Safari and Firefox on phones and computers. Browsers with a built-in barcode reader (Chrome on Android and macOS) use it directly; others download an open-source decoder (ZXing, compiled to WebAssembly, about 1 MB from the jsDelivr CDN) the first time you scan. The camera needs an https page and your permission.
faq.installQuestion: Can I install the scanner as an app?
faq.installAnswer: Yes. Use your browser's Install or Add to Home Screen option on this page to get a scanner icon that opens straight to the camera.

faq.accountQuestion: Do I need a QRdx account?
faq.accountAnswer: No. The plugins are free and work without an account. Each one links to the full editor at qrdx.dev (Open in QRdx in Chrome and Raycast, More options in Figma and Canva), where you can sign in for dynamic codes you can edit after printing.
faq.dataQuestion: Do the plugins send my data anywhere?
faq.dataAnswer: The Chrome extension and the Figma plugin make no network requests: codes are drawn on your device by the qrdx library. The Raycast extension keeps saved codes in Raycast's local storage, and Generate QR with AI sends your description to Raycast AI. The Canva app draws the code in its panel and adds it to your design as an image. When you open the playground from a plugin, only a web address goes along, after the # in the link, which browsers never send to a server.
faq.changeQuestion: Can I change a code after adding it?
faq.changeAnswer: In Figma, select it and click Edit QR code, or use Replace selected QR to keep its size and position. In Raycast, saved codes can be edited and exported again. In Chrome and Canva, make a new code; for printed codes whose link you want to change later, use a dynamic code from the QRdx dashboard.
